sec.title: Background
sec.p: Thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy (TAO) is a thyroid function-related, organ-specific autoimmune disease that primarily leads to specific reactive changes and tissue remodeling in the periocular region. The exact pathogenesis of TAO remains unclear.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: High-throughput gene expression datasets related to TAO were comprehensively retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database, selecting GSE174139 and GSE158464 for analysis. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between TAO patients and healthy controls were identified, and ferroptosis-related genes (FRGs) were obtained from the FerrDb database. The intersection of DEGs and FRGs yielded ferroptosis-related genes associated with TAO.The transcriptional expression of FRGs was validated using real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) on orbital adipose tissue samples from TAO patients and healthy controls. Single-cell sequencing of six human tissue samples further analyzed changes in cellular subpopulations within the TAO microenvironment.Additionally, a co-culture model of CD163 + macrophages and TAO orbital fibroblasts, along with an in vitro TGF-β1-induced orbital fibroblast (OF) model, was constructed to validate the role of the TGF-β1/SMAD2/3 axis in ferroptosis regulation. Finally, potential clinical drugs targeting CD163 + macrophages with high ferroptosis activity in TAO were predicted using the Random Walk with Restart (RWR) algorithm combined with the DGIdb database.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: We first utilized TAO-related datasets from the GEO database, combined with the FerrDb ferroptosis database, to identify changes in iron metabolism genes during TAO progression through differential expression analysis, screening 7 key ferroptosis-related proteins. In vitro validation revealed that all but AOPQ and LGMN, which were upregulated, exhibited downregulated expression.Single-cell sequencing of orbital connective tissue from 4 TAO patients and 2 healthy controls identified 16,364 cells spanning 18 cell types. Analysis of the 7 key ferroptosis-related proteins revealed that fibroblasts and macrophages displayed elevated ferroptosis signaling during TAO progression. Subcluster analysis of macrophages identified 4 distinct subpopulations, with the C2 subpopulation—characterized by high expression of CD163 and CCL18—exhibiting prominent ferroptosis activation signals.Further validation using clinical tissue samples, a co-culture model of CD163 + macrophages and TAO orbital fibroblasts, and an in vitro TGF-β1-induced orbital fibroblast (OF) model confirmed aberrant activation of the TGF-β1/SMAD2/3 pathway as a key regulator of ferroptosis. Hub gene analysis of C2 subpopulation marker genes, combined with the DGIdb database, predicted potential clinical drugs targeting the C2 macrophages.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study, integrating single-cell RNA-Seq and bulk transcriptome analysis, revealed the involvement of CD163 + tissue-infiltrating macrophages in regulating ferroptosis of orbital fibroblasts during TAO progression and identified therapeutic candidates targeting macrophage ferroptosis signaling in TAO. Furthermore, in vitro experiments demonstrated that activation of the TGF-β1/SMAD2/3 axis promotes ferroptosis in TAO orbital fibroblasts, highlighting a novel pathway for potential therapeutic intervention.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy (TAO) is an autoimmune orbital disease related to thyroid dysfunction, primarily affecting the eye and retro-orbital tissues. It poses a serious threat to vision, alters the appearance of the eye, and significantly impacts quality of life [1, 2]. TAO is commonly secondary to Graves’ disease (GD), with an incidence of approximately 25–50% in GD patients, but it can also be observed in conditions such as Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, hypothyroidism, and even in euthyroid individuals [3, 4]. The clinical manifestations of TAO are diverse and vary significantly among patients, typically involving the extraocular muscles and orbital fat. Symptoms include proptosis, eyelid retraction, upper eyelid lag, ocular motility disturbances, conjunctival congestion and edema, and even exposure keratopathy and compressive optic neuropathy, all of which affect the patient’s appearance and vision. In severe cases, TAO can lead to blindness [5, 6]. Despite the availability of various medications and radiation therapies for TAO [7–9], these treatments are effective in only a subset of patients. A significant proportion of patients still require multiple ocular reconstructive surgeries due to poor therapeutic outcomes.

The pathogenesis of TAO remains unclear, though previous studies suggest that oxidative stress and orbital tissue remodeling are key pathological changes in the disease. Target tissues and cells are generally found to be in a state of oxidative stress, with excessive production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), including hydroxyl radicals, hydrogen peroxide, superoxide anions, and lipid peroxides, all of which have highly reactive properties due to unpaired electrons [10–12]. The imbalance between increased ROS production and reduced ROS clearance leads to oxidative stress and disrupts cellular homeostasis [13]. Ferroptosis, a recently discovered iron-dependent form of programmed cell death, is characterized by iron overload and the accumulation of lipid peroxides, and is closely linked to oxidative stress [14]. Current research has shown that ferroptosis plays a role in the pathogenesis of a variety of diseases, including cancer, inflammatory diseases, autoimmune disorders, cardiovascular diseases, metabolic diseases, and neurodegenerative diseases [15]. Notably, studies by Ye et al. have indicated that abnormal expression of ferroptosis-related genes significantly impacts the development of TAO [16]. However, despite considerable research on the role of ferroptosis in disease mechanisms and drug development, its relationship with TAO is still in its early stages. Further investigation of the mechanisms of ferroptosis in TAO could uncover new therapeutic targets.

It is well-established that the onset of TAO is associated with complex interactions between cytokines such as IFN-γ, CXCL-8, and TNF-α, which ultimately lead to immune cell infiltration in the orbit and activation of orbital fibroblast (OF) proliferation. OFs are the key effector cells in TAO, and the changes in immune cell infiltration and their interactions with OFs play a crucial role in regulating local inflammation and tissue remodeling [17]. Recent studies have identified a subset of CD34 + CXCR4 + Col1 + monocyte-derived OFs that express elevated levels of thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor (TSHR) and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) receptors [18]. In addition, previous research using single-cell transcriptomics has identified the presence of a TAO-specific CD4 + cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) population, suggesting a potential link between the expansion of this subset, their strong cytotoxic response to self-antigens, localization in orbital tissues, and disease relapse [19]. Furthermore, Wang et al. recently used single-cell sequencing to identify the expansion of the CD169 + classical monocyte population in TAO, demonstrating that these CD169 + monocyte-derived macrophages may contribute to excessive inflammation, fibrosis, and adipogenesis in the orbit [18]. Although previous studies have focused mainly on moderate-to-severe inactive phase TAO patients, the mechanisms by which immune cell changes regulate orbital inflammation and tissue remodeling remain unclear.

Current research suggests that CD14 + monocytes are associated with changes in immune cell infiltration in TAO orbital tissues, differentiating primarily into macrophages and dendritic cells, which regulate immune responses and may exacerbate the disease [20]. Macrophages are phagocytic immune cells widely distributed across tissues and organs, playing important roles in immune response, tissue homeostasis, and remodeling. Macrophages exhibit considerable heterogeneity, and their phenotypes and functions are regulated by the surrounding microenvironment. Based on activation conditions, they can be classified into two subtypes: M1 macrophages activated via the classical pathway and M2 macrophages activated via the alternative pathway [21, 22]. Recent studies have shown that macrophages play a critical role in regulating iron metabolism, with different macrophage subtypes exhibiting distinct iron metabolic processes. Conversely, iron metabolism can also regulate macrophage functional states. Previous studies have indicated that CD169 + macrophages promote excessive inflammation, fibrosis, and adipogenesis in the orbit, but whether infiltrating macrophages in TAO regulate ferroptosis in orbital fibroblasts and contribute to fibrosis and adipogenesis in orbital tissues remains largely unknown.

Single-cell transcriptomics, which involves high-throughput sequencing of the transcriptomes of individual cells, is a powerful tool for revealing gene expression profiles at the single-cell level and reflecting cellular heterogeneity. In this study, we aim to explore the regulation of ferroptosis and changes in microenvironmental components during the progression of TAO using single-cell RNA-Seq combined with bulk transcriptomic analysis. We will also investigate the role of tissue-infiltrating macrophages in regulating ferroptosis in orbital fibroblasts during TAO pathogenesis and identify potential therapeutic targets.

sec.title: Data download and preprocessing
sec.p: The bulk datasets GSE174139 (samples GSM5287845-GSM5287848) and GSE158464 (samples GSM4801165-GSM4801166) were downloaded after normalization, totaling 6 samples (Table S1). Protein-coding genes were selected for analysis using the Ensembl database. Ferroptosis-related gene sets were downloaded from the FerrDb database, which includes 348 inhibitory genes and 369 driver genes. Protein-protein interaction data were obtained from the STRING database, and the interaction network was visualized using Cytoscape.

sec.title: Differential gene expression analysis
sec.p: Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using DESeq2 with a threshold of p.adj < 0.05 and |log2FoldChange| > 0.5. Gene IDs were converted using the Ensembl database.

sec.title: Enrichment analysis
sec.p: Enrichment analysis was performed using the R package clusterProfiler, with the parameters ont = “BP” and minGSSize = 5.

sec.title: Single-cell data analysis
sec.p: Raw FASTQ data were aligned to the reference genome GRCh38 using Cellranger 6.1.1. Data integration and analysis were carried out using Seurat version 4.0.5. Low-quality cells, defined as those with fewer than 1000 detected genes or with more than 10% mitochondrial genes, were filtered out. Data from different samples were integrated using the IntegrateData function, and cell clusters were identified by finding marker genes using the FindAllMarkers function. Cell interaction analysis was performed using cellphonedb version 2.0.

sec.title: Identification of ferroptosis-active cells
sec.p: Ferroptosis scores for single cells were calculated using the default parameters of the AUCell package. Using the 7 ferroptosis-related differential genes from the bulk transcriptome, cells were ranked by gene expression using the AUCell_buildRankings function. The AUCell_calcAUC function was used to calculate the AUC values for each cell, and the AUCell_exploreThresholds function was used to determine the optimal threshold for ferroptosis gene activation.

sec.title: Identification of hub genes using restarted walk network algorithm
sec.p: Based on the protein interaction information for human proteins from the STRING database, we used the marker genes of macrophage C2 subpopulations as seed genes and applied the restarted random walk network algorithm using the dnet R package to calculate affinity scores, assessing the degree of information convergence. To identify hub genes, we randomly selected an equal number of seed genes (1000 iterations) and selected genes with an affinity score greater than the 95th percentile of the top 100 scores across all iterations as hub genes.

sec.title: Gene and drug prediction analysis
sec.p: Using the DGIdb database, gene-drug interactions were explored for the top 100 hub genes. Drugs or small molecules that were associated with at least three genes or had interactions with at least three of the selected hub genes were recorded.

sec.title: Collection of human orbital fat tissue
sec.p: Orbital fat tissue was obtained from TAO patients in the stable phase who underwent orbital decompression surgery at the affiliated Eye Hospital of Nanchang University. The patients were aged between 18 and 65 years. Control tissue samples were collected from patients undergoing blepharoplasty and eye bag surgery at the same hospital. The tissue was collected from the excised orbital fat during surgery. This study was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles outlined by the Helsinki Declaration and was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Eye Hospital of Nanchang University (Approval number: YLS20231020).

sec.title: Cultivation of M0 and CD163 + macrophages
sec.p: In this study, THP-1 cells were cultured in DMEM complete medium containing 10% FBS (SA101.02, Cellmax, China) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin. When cell density reached 80%, cells were collected at a density of approximately 3.5 × 10^5 cells/mL into six-well plates. Subsequently, 100 ng/mL PMA was added, and the cells were treated in an incubator with PMA for 48 h to induce differentiation into macrophages. The cells were then washed three times with PBS and cultured in DMEM complete medium supplemented with IL-4 (20 ng/mL) and IL-13 (20 ng/mL) for 72 h to polarize them into CD163 + macrophages.

After obtaining M0 macrophages and CD163 + macrophages using the method described above, cells were washed three times with PBS and fresh DMEM complete medium was added. After 24 h, supernatants were collected for further analysis.

sec.title: Cultivation and intervention of human orbital fibroblasts (OFs)
sec.p: Adipose tissue obtained during surgery was placed into a sterile 15 mL centrifuge tube and transported to the laboratory as quickly as possible. The tissue was cut into small fat blocks approximately 1 mm³ in size using scissors and dispersed in culture dishes. Complete medium (DMEM [Vivacell Biosciences, C3110-1500, China] + 20% FBS [10099-141-c, Gibco, Australia] + 1% penicillin-streptomycin [P1400, Solarbio, China]) was added.

After 3–7 days, cells began to migrate from the tissue blocks. Once a sufficient number of cells had migrated around the tissue fragments, the tissue blocks were removed. By 5–7 days post-extraction, approximately 80–90% cell confluence was achieved.

To investigate the effect of CD163 + macrophages on OF ferroptosis, fifth-passage orbital fibroblasts (OFs) were seeded into six-well plates. When cell confluence reached 80–90%, they were co-cultured with CD163 + macrophages for 72 h using transwell inserts (0.4 μm). Following co-culture, RT-PCR and Western blot experiments were performed.

Subsequently, the effect of TGF-β1 (HY-P70543, MedChemExpress, China) on OFs was explored. Cells were cultured in complete medium containing 5 ng/mL TGF-β1 for 24 h, followed by RT-PCR and Western blot experiments.

sec.title: Cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8) assay
sec.p: Orbital fibroblasts (OFS) from the 5th generation were seeded at a density of 1 × 10^4 cells/well in a 96-well plate and cultured for 24 h. To explore the optimal intervention time for macrophages to influence OFs, macrophage supernatants were used to intervene in OFs for 24, 48, and 72 h, respectively. To explore the optimal intervention concentration of TGF-β1 to intervene in OFs, cells were treated with different concentrations of TGF-β 1(0 ng/ml, 2.5 ng/ml, 3.5 ng/ml, 5.0 ng/ml, 7.5 ng/ml, 10 ng/ml, 12.5 ng/ml) for 24 h. After carrying out the above treatments, 10% CCK-8 in complete culture medium was added to each well, and cells were incubated at 37 °C for 1–4 h. The absorbance at 450 nm was measured using a microplate reader to quantify cell viability.

sec.title: RT-PCR
sec.p: Total RNA from tissues and cells was extracted using the AG RNAex Pro RNA extraction kit (AG21101, ACCURATE BIOTECHNOLOGY (HUNAN) CO., LTD., Changsha, China). The RNA was then purified using the Steady Pure RNA Purification kit (AG21024, ACCURATE BIOTECHNOLOGY (HUNAN) CO., LTD., Changsha, China). Purified RNA was reverse-transcribed into cDNA using the Evo M-MLV RT PreMix Kit (AG11728, ACCURATE BIOTECHNOLOGY (HUNAN) CO., LTD., Changsha, China). SYBR Green Pro Taq HS qPCR reagent kit (AG11701, ACCURATE BIOTECHNOLOGY (HUNAN) CO., LTD., Changsha, China) was used for amplification. Fluorescence signals were collected and analyzed during the exponential amplification phase. All results were analyzed based on three independent experiments, each performed in triplicate.Primer information is detailed in Table S2-S3.

sec.title: Western blot
sec.p: Cell and tissue lysates were prepared using RIPA buffer (Solarbio, China) and separated by SDS-PAGE before being transferred to PVDF membranes. The membranes were blocked with 5% non-fat milk for 1.5 h and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies: CP1 (Proteintech, 66156-1-Ig, 1:1000), NQO1 (Proteintech, 11451-1-AP, 1:4000), FTL (Proteintech, 10727-1-AP, 1:4000), AQP3 (Huabio, ER1903-84, 1:500), LGMN (Proteintech, 67017-1-Ig, 1:2000), and MGST1 (Huabio, EM1901-13, 1:1000). After incubation with secondary antibody (Boster, BA1050, 1:8000) for 1 h at room temperature, Western blotting was performed using WesternBright ECL (Advansta, USA). Images were captured using a chemiluminescence imaging system (Tanon-5200 Multi, China) and quantified using ImageJ software.

sec.title: Flow cytometry
sec.p: To detect macrophage polarization status, FITC Mouse Anti-Human CD68 (BD Pharmingen, USA, 562117) was used as a surface marker for M0 macrophages. To identify the C2 subpopulation as CD163 + macrophages, FITC Mouse Anti-Human CD163 (BD Pharmingen, USA, 563697) was selected to label the C2 macrophage subpopulation.

THP-1 cells and polarized macrophages were suspended in 5% FBS. These cells were then incubated with anti-CD68 and anti-CD163 antibodies in the dark for 30 min. After incubation, the cells were washed three times with FBS and analyzed within 2 h using a CytoFlex flow cytometer. The resulting images were assessed using FlowJo software.

sec.title: Immunofluorescence
sec.p: For identification of orbital fibroblasts (OFS), 5th generation OFS cells were seeded at a density of 1 × 10^5 cells/well in a 24-well plate and grown to 70-80% confluence. Cells were fixed with ice-cold methanol and blocked with 3% BSA (A8020, Solarbio, China) for 1 h at room temperature. Cells were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies: α-SMA (14395-1-AP, Proteintech, China), fibronectin (15163-1-AP, Proteintech, China), vimentin (60330-1-Ig, Proteintech, China), and cytokeratin-19 (10712-1-AP, Proteintech, China). After washing with PBS, cells were incubated for 1 h at room temperature with fluorescein II antibody (Servicebio, GB25301, 1:500) and then stained with DAPI (Solarbio, C0065) for 10 min. Images were captured using a confocal microscope.

To identify CD163 + macrophage expression in TAO patient orbital fat tissue, paraffin sections of orbital fat tissue were deparaffinized and subjected to antigen retrieval with 1× EDTA at heated conditions. After cooling to room temperature, sections were washed with PBS three times for 5 min each. Sections were blocked with normal serum at room temperature for 1 h, followed by washing three times with PBS. The sections were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibody CD163 (Proteintech, 68218-1-Ig, 1:500). After washing with PBS, fluorescein II antibody (Servicebio, GB25301, 1:500) was applied for 1 h at room temperature in the dark. Sections were washed again with PBS and stained with DAPI (Solarbio, C0065), mounted, and stored at 4 °C. Images were captured using a confocal microscope.

sec.title: Identification of ferroptosis signaling activation in TAO based on bulk data
sec.p: Based on RNA-seq data related to TAO from the public GEO database, including 6 samples, differential gene expression analysis was performed using DESeq2 with the criteria padj < 0.05 and |log2FoldChange| > 0.5, identifying a total of 334 differentially expressed genes (Fig. 1A). A comparative analysis with the ferroptosis-related database FerrDb revealed seven ferroptosis-associated genes: the ferroptosis driver genes AQP3 and LGMN, and the suppressor genes CP, FTL, MGST1, NQO1, and TMSB4X (Fig. 1B). These genes were downregulated during TAO disease progression, suggesting activation of ferroptosis signaling (Fig. 1C).

caption.p: Transcriptomic changes associated with ferroptosis in the progression of TAO based on bulk data analysis. (A) Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the TAO disease group were calculated based on GEO public data. (B) Venn diagram showing the intersection between TAO DEGs and ferroptosis-related genes from the FerrDb database, revealing 7 ferroptosis-associated genes linked to TAO. (C) Heatmap illustrating the expression levels of the 7 ferroptosis-related genes in the normal and disease groups of TAO. (D) Protein-protein interaction (PPI) network based on STRING database information, displaying differentially expressed genes in TAO that interact with the 7 ferroptosis-related genes. (E) Gene expression correlation analysis showing the transcriptomic correlations of genes with the 7 ferroptosis-related genes

sec.p: To identify key genes involved in ferroptosis during TAO progression, we performed further analysis using the STRING database to construct a protein-protein interaction (PPI) network in combination with gene expression correlation analysis. Genes with both significant protein-level interactions and notable RNA expression correlations (FDR < 0.05, |R| > 0.7) were selected. The results showed that all seven ferroptosis-related genes interacted with various differentially expressed genes in TAO, with FTL and TMSB4X showing the closest associations with other genes (Fig. 1D-E). These findings suggest abnormal activation of the ferroptosis signaling pathway during TAO progression.

To assess the mRNA levels of these key genes, we used orbital adipose tissue from TAO patients undergoing orbital decompression surgery as the experimental group and orbital adipose tissue from patients undergoing ocular plastic surgery as the control group. RT-PCR was performed to measure the expression of differentially expressed ferroptosis-related genes (FRGs) and TGF-β in both groups (Fig. 2A-D, Fig. S2). The results showed that, except for LGMN and AQP3 which were upregulated, the other FRGs exhibited downregulated mRNA expression. For several FRGs, protein expression levels were further explored using Western blot analysis (Fig. 2E-H), which revealed that, except for an increase in LGMN expression, FTL, CP1, NQO1, and MGST1 showed reduced expression in TAO orbital adipose tissue. Although AQP3 was upregulated, the difference was not statistically significant. Additionally, the expression of the SMAD2/3 axis proteins in TAO orbital adipose tissue was investigated (Fig. 2I-J), showing decreased SMAD2/3 expression and increased P-SMAD2/3 expression in TAO tissue.

(D)Transcriptional levels of TGF-β in orbital adipose tissue(E-H) Translational levels of selected ferroptosis-related genes in orbital adipose tissue. (I-J) Translational levels of SMAD2/3 and P-SMAD2/3 in orbital adipose tissue.(Notes:The transcript levels and protein levels of these FRGs were normalized to GAPDH. Statistical significance was determined by the Student’s t-test. Results are presented as mean ± SEM. n = 3; ns: p > 0.05, *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, ****p < 0.0001)

sec.title: Single-cell atlas of TAO patients
sec.p: To further elucidate the regulatory mechanism of ferroptosis signaling during TAO progression, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing on eye tissues from 2 normal volunteers and 4 TAO patients. The sequencing data were aligned to the reference genome GRCh38 using Cellranger-6.1.1, with quality control based on the criteria of more than 1000 genes detected per cell and mitochondrial gene expression below 10%. Single-cell data analysis was conducted under the Seurat framework, and data from different samples were integrated using the IntegrateData function. A total of 16,364 cells across 6 samples were identified, representing 18 cell types (Fig. 3A-B), including fibroblasts, arterial endothelial cells (AEC), capillary endothelial cells (CEC), venous endothelial cells (VEC1, VEC2), pericytes (PC), B cells, T cells, NK cells, NKT cells, neutrophils (Neu), mast cells, monocytes (Mono), dendritic cells (DC), myeloid dendritic cells (mDC), plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDC), and mitotic cells (Mito). Marker genes for each cell type were computed(Fig. S3), and the top 10 markers specific to each cell type were displayed (Fig. 3C).

caption.p: Single-cell transcriptomic atlas of TAO patients. (A) Single-cell sequencing and cell type annotation of ocular connective tissue from 2 healthy individuals and 4 TAO patients. (B) Annotation results of 18 cell types in the healthy and TAO groups, respectively. (C) Characteristic genes used for cell type annotation, based on previous research reports. (D) Distribution of cell type proportions across the 6 individual samples.(E) AUCell-based assessment of 7 ferroptosis-related genes to identify cells with activated ferroptosis signaling.(F) Proportion of cells with activated ferroptosis signaling in each cell type. (G) The changes in cell proportions during the course of Thyroid-Associated Ophthalmopathy

sec.p: Cell proportion analysis revealed that neutrophils (Neu) and a group of venous endothelial cells (VEC2) were exclusively present in the TAO group, suggesting inflammation-related cell infiltration during TAO progression and highlighting the key role of immune cells in the disease process (Fig. 3D). Through further analysis, 250 macrophages were identified, with their cell count being relatively low compared to parenchymal cells. To explore the relationship between cell types and ferroptosis, we used the previous 7 genes for AUCell scoring to assess the ferroptosis signal activation in each cell type. The results showed that macrophages and fibroblasts had the closest relationship with ferroptosis signal activation (Fig. 3E-F). Additionally, Analysis of cell proportions in single-cell transcriptome data was performed to show changes in cell proportions in healthy control and disease groups separately, with statistical p-values using the non-parametric wilcox test. The results showed an increase in the cell proportion of macrophages (Mac) in the disease group. (Fig. 3G). Therefore, subgroup analysis of macrophages is helpful in exploring the underlying cellular and molecular changes during the progression of TAO.

sec.title: Subgroup analysis of ferroptosis in macrophages in TAO
sec.p: To further explore the mechanism of ferroptosis in macrophages, we performed subgroup analysis of the macrophages. The results revealed four macrophage subgroups, C1-C4 (Fig. 4A), and these four subgroups were found in higher numbers in the TAO group (Fig. 4B). Marker gene analysis of these subgroups was conducted, and the top 10 markers specific to each cell type were displayed (Fig. 4C-D). The C1 subgroup exhibited high expression of HLA family genes and immunoglobulin IgE receptor FCER1A, indicating that C1 macrophages have higher antigen-presenting and immune-regulatory activity. The C2 subgroup was characterized by high expression of CD163 and CCL18 genes, displaying features of inflammation suppression. The C3 subgroup showed high expression of IL1B and TLR2 genes, which, upon activation, produce reactive oxygen species that activate the cell’s own antioxidant signaling. The C4 subgroup exhibited high expression of CD68 and the pro-inflammatory factor SPP1, activating oxidative stress responses and promoting macrophage activation and migration (Fig. 4C-D).

caption.p: Subgroup analysis of macrophages in TAO patients. (A) UMAP plot displaying the four macrophage subgroups. (B) Distribution of the four macrophage subgroups in the UMAP plot for both healthy controls and TAO patients. (C) Feature genes for the four macrophage subgroups, identified based on prior studies and FindAllMarkers analysis. (D) Top 10 marker genes specific to each macrophage subgroup, as determined by FindAllMarkers. (E) Enrichment analysis of all the marker genes for the four macrophage subgroups (p.adj < 0.05, |log2FC| > 0.25), with the key terms displayed

sec.p: To further investigate the relationship between cell subtypes and ferroptosis, we conducted enrichment analysis on all marker genes of the four macrophage subgroups. The C1 subgroup was associated with T cell activation and antigen presentation via MHC II, C2 with cell death and oxidative stress, C3 with neutrophil activation and acute inflammatory responses, and C4 with neutrophil activation and antigen presentation via MHC I (Fig. 4E). Therefore, we hypothesize that the C2 subgroup may be the key macrophage subset driving TAO progression.

We validated, using tissue immunofluorescence, that the infiltration of CD163 + macrophages in the orbital adipose tissue of TAO patients was higher compared to normal controls (Fig. 5K-L). We also constructed a CD163 + macrophage model in vitro, which exhibited larger cell bodies and surface spiky protrusions (Fig. 5A-C). Further validation was conducted via RT-PCR and flow cytometry (Fig. 5D, E, G-J). RT-PCR results showed a significant upregulation of the M0 macrophage marker CD11b and the CD163 + macrophage marker CD163 mRNA expression. Flow cytometry analysis revealed a rightward shift in the fluorescence peaks for M0 macrophage marker CD68 and CD163 + macrophage marker CD163, with a significant increase in mean fluorescence intensity. Additionally, we verified the mRNA expression of TGF-β in CD163 + macrophages, which was significantly elevated (Fig. 5F).

sec.title: Macrophage subpopulation interaction analysis
sec.p: We performed AUCell scoring of the four macrophage subtypes using the seven ferroptosis-related genes mentioned earlier and found that macrophage subtype C2 exhibited significantly higher ferroptosis activation signals (Fig. 6A-B). Furthermore, we conducted a correlation analysis between the seven ferroptosis-related genes and the marker genes of the four macrophage subtypes. The results revealed that CCL-18 correlated with multiple ferroptosis-related genes, further confirming the close association of the CCL-18-high expressing macrophage C2 subtype with ferroptosis signaling during TAO progression (Fig. 6C). Subsequently, we performed intercellular communication analysis using CellphoneDB 2.0.0. The analysis showed increased interactions between macrophage C2 and various cells during TAO progression, such as the association of increased TNF signaling with ferroptosis activation (Fig. 6D). Additionally, the downregulated cell interactions primarily involved the TGF-β signaling pathway, which is closely linked to ferroptosis suppression (Fig. 6E). These findings indicate an imbalance in the ferroptosis regulation of macrophage C2 during TAO progression. Further statistical analysis of the intercellular interactions revealed that macrophages mainly interacted with neutrophils and venous endothelial cells, with the C2 subtype showing particularly pronounced signals (Fig. 6F). A protein interaction network analysis of all marker genes of the C2 subtype revealed a tight interaction between the C2-specific genes and key factors, including JUN, FOS, HSP90AA1, HSP90AB1 and HSPA8, suggesting the potential of these genes as key targets for intervening in TAO progression (Fig. 6G).

sec.p: This study collected primary cells cultured in vitro from orbital adipose tissue (Fig. S4A-B), which were then identified as orbital adipose-derived fibroblasts (OFs) using immunofluorescence (Fig. S4C-F). The results showed positive staining for fibronectin antibody, α-SMA antibody, vimentin antibody, negative staining for cytokeratin-19 antibody.

We performed a temporal gradient CCK8 experiment of the effect of CD163 + macrophage supernatant on OFs, and the results showed that at 48 h of intervention, the cell activity was higher than that at 24 h and 72 h, so we used 48 h as the optimal time of intervention for OFs to interact with CD163 + macrophages(Fig. 7A).We co-cultured CD163 + macrophages with orbital adipose OFs in Transwell chambers (0.4 μm) and analyzed the expression of ferroptosis-related genes (FRGs) in OFs after 48 h. The results (Fig. 7B-C, Fig.S5) demonstrated that the transcription and translation levels of FTL, NQO1, and MGST1 were reduced in OFs upon intervention with CD163 + macrophages, while LGMN exhibited a decrease in transcription level but an increase in translation level. Although there were differences in the translation levels of other FRGs, they were not statistically significant. Furthermore, the translation levels of SMAD2/3 were reduced in OFs after CD163 + macrophage intervention (Fig. 7D).

(D) Translational expression of SMAD2/3.(E) CCK8 assay quantifying cell viability after treatment with different concentrations of TGF-β1. (F-J) Transcriptional levels of selected FRGs in OFs after treatment with 5 ng/ml TGF-β1. (K-L) Translational levels of two FRGs in OFs after treatment with 5 ng/ml TGF-β1. (M-N) Translational levels of SMAD2/3 and P-SMAD2/3 in OFs after treatment with 5 ng/ml TGF-β1.(Notes: The transcript levels of these FRGs was normalized to GAPDH, and the protein levels of these FRGs were normalized to GAPDH or β-actin. The statistical significance of differences was calculated by the Student’s t-test. The results are presented as the mean ± SEM. n = 3; ns: p > 0.05, *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ***P < 0.0001)

sec.p: To further investigate the impact of TGF-β on ferroptosis in cell interactions, we determined the optimal concentration of TGF-β1 for intervention in orbital adipose OFs using CCK8 assays. The results showed that cell viability increased to a plateau at 5 ng/ml TGF-β1 (Fig. 7E). Based on this, 5 ng/ml TGF-β1 was selected as the modeling concentration to intervene in orbital adipose OFs. After 48 h, we extracted RNA and protein from the cells to observe the expression of FRGs (Fig. 7F-L, Fig S6). The results indicated that, under TGF-β1 intervention, the mRNA expression of most FRGs decreased, except for TMSB4X and LGMN, which were upregulated. Additionally, the protein expression of FTL, NQO1, and MGST1 decreased, while the protein levels of LGMN and AQP3 were elevated. However, the differences in translation levels of other FRGs were not statistically significant. Finally, the SMAD2/3 axis was examined, and the results showed a decrease in the protein expression of SMAD2/3 and an increase in P-SMAD2/3 expression in OFs after 5 ng/ml TGF-β1 intervention (Fig. 7M-N), which was consistent with the expression pattern observed in TAO orbital adipose tissue.

sec.title: Macrophage ferroptosis hub genes and drug screening
sec.p: Furthermore, we employed the markers of macrophage C2 as seed genes to perform a restart-based random walk in the protein-protein interaction network, aiming to identify hub genes driving the ferroptosis signaling in macrophage C2. Hub genes were identified using the default parameters of the R dnet package, with 1000 randomly selected gene sets of equal size as the background distribution. Genes with scores higher than the 95th percentile of the 1000 random selections were considered significantly converged hub genes. The top 100 genes are shown as potential hub genes (Fig. 8A), with CD163 and LGMN consistent with previous findings. To explore the ferroptosis characteristics of macrophage C2, we analyzed the interactions between the top hub genes and drugs based on the DGIdb database. The results revealed that HSP90AA1, HSP90AB1, and CSF1R interact with multiple drugs, suggesting them as potential therapeutic targets for TAO (Fig. 8B).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: TAO is a thyroid-related, organ-specific autoimmune disease with a complex pathogenesis, involving inflammation, cytokine production, hyaluronan synthesis, adipogenesis, and myofibrosis [23, 24]. Ferroptosis, characterized by lipid peroxidation and iron overload, is linked to alterations in various metabolic pathways, including iron, glucose, and lipid metabolism [14]. In this study, we performed differential expression analysis of TAO-related RNA-seq data from six GEO samples and compared them with the Ferroptosis database FerrDb. We identified seven ferroptosis-associated genes (AQP3, LGMN, CP1, FTL, MGST1, NQO1, and TMSB4X) that were consistently downregulated during the progression of TAO. Protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis through STRING revealed interactions between these genes and other differentially expressed genes in TAO, with FTL and TMSB4X showing tight associations. We validated these findings in clinical samples from three patients with severe inactive phase TAO and three healthy controls, where, except for LGMN, the expression of CP1, FTL, MGST1, and NQO1 was downregulated, suggesting abnormal activation of ferroptosis in the orbital adipose tissue of TAO patients.

Ferritin, composed of FTL (light chain) and FTH1 (heavy chain), is a major intracellular iron storage protein complex that plays a pivotal role in regulating cellular iron metabolism [25–27]. Iron is transported into cells and stored in FTH1/FTL complexes, with FTH1/FTL-mediated ferritin autophagy releasing iron when iron is scarce [28, 29]. Ceruloplasmin (CP), a multicopper oxidase, is considered an effective antioxidant by promoting the efflux of Fe2 + through the iron exporter FPN1, inhibiting ROS generation [30–32]. NQO1, an antioxidant enzyme, helps maintain redox balance and energy metabolism, and its downregulation can promote ferroptosis [33–35]. MGST1, which helps protect cellular membranes from lipid peroxidation and oxidative stress, has been shown to inhibit ferroptosis by binding ALOX5 and preventing lipid peroxidation [36–38]. LGMN, involved in immune cell infiltration, encodes Legumain, a protein involved in immune response [39, 40]. Recent studies suggest that LGMN participates in ferroptosis through lysosomal autophagy in renal tubules [41]. In our study, the downregulation of genes inhibiting ferroptosis and the upregulation of LGMN further support the hypothesis of abnormal ferroptosis activation in the orbital tissues of TAO patients.

Recently, several studies have reported that ferroptosis-related genes are associated with immune infiltrating cells (especially monocytes) in Thyroid-Associated Ophthalmopathy (TAO) [42]. Therefore, we further explored the regulatory mechanisms of ferroptosis signaling during the progression of TAO through single-cell RNA sequencing of ocular tissues from normal volunteers and TAO patients. We identified neutrophils (Neu) and a group of venous endothelial cells (VEC2) exclusively in the TAO group, suggesting the presence of inflammatory cell infiltration during TAO progression and highlighting the critical role of immune cells in the disease’s progression. AUCell scoring of ferroptosis-related genes downregulated in TAO revealed elevated ferroptosis activity in fibroblasts and macrophages. To further investigate the relationship between cell subtypes and ferroptosis, we performed subgroup analysis of macrophages and enrichment analysis of marker genes across four macrophage subgroups. The C2 subgroup was found to be associated with cell death and oxidative stress. Thus, we propose that C2 may be a key macrophage subset driving TAO progression. Additionally, AUCell scoring of seven ferroptosis-related genes in these macrophage subgroups confirmed that CD163 + macrophages in the C2 subtype exhibit heightened ferroptosis activation signals. CD163 is a scavenger receptor that interacts with hemoglobin-haptoglobin complexes and is primarily used as a specific marker for macrophages, especially C2-like cells [43]. Previous studies have demonstrated that CD163 and SLC40A1 are selectively expressed in C2-like macrophages in lupus nephritis, with a strong association to iron homeostasis [44]. Cheng et al. also reported that the abnormal increase of CD163 + tissue-infiltrating macrophages could lead to excessive phagocytosis of hemoglobin-haptoglobin complexes, which may result in excessive iron accumulation within macrophages and increased unstable iron pools, ultimately causing oxidative stress and ferroptosis [45]. Therefore, we conducted immunofluorescence analysis of CD163 + macrophages in orbital adipose tissue from TAO patients and healthy controls. The results showed an increased infiltration of CD163 + macrophages and elevated CCL-18 expression in TAO patient tissues. Further, after co-culturing orbital fibroblasts (OFs) with CD163 + macrophages and extracting RNA and protein, we confirmed that, besides the upregulation of LGMN, the expression of MGST1 and FTL was downregulated. Although NQO1 exhibited a trend of downregulation, it did not reach statistical significance. These findings further validated that the C2 macrophage subtype indeed harbors elevated ferroptosis activation signals.

Due to the complex intercellular interactions, to further explore the potential signaling pathways by which C2 macrophages regulate ferroptosis in orbital fibroblasts (OFs), we performed intercellular communication analysis using CellphoneDB 2.0.0. The analysis revealed that during the progression of Thyroid-Associated Ophthalmopathy (TAO), C2 macrophages interacted with a variety of cells, with increased TNF signaling potentially associated with ferroptosis activation. In addition, the downregulation of cell interactions that inhibit ferroptosis mainly involved the TGF-β signaling pathway, which is also closely linked to the aberrant activation of ferroptosis. Kim et al. found that TGF-β can activate the expression of xCT in hepatocellular carcinoma cells via Smad3, inducing lipid peroxidation and increasing vulnerability to GPX4 inhibition, thus promoting ferroptosis [46]. Huang et al. demonstrated that TGF-β plays a crucial role in mediating apoptosis and ferroptosis in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)/D-GalN-induced acute liver failure (ALF) [47]. Recent studies have shown that TGF-β stimulation upregulates the expression of transferrin receptor 1 (TFRC) in both human lung fibroblast cell line (MRC-5) and primary murine lung fibroblasts, leading to elevated intracellular Fe2 + levels and promoting fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition [48–50]. Clinical tissue samples and in vitro experiments further confirmed that after TGF-β treatment, besides CP1, other ferroptosis inhibitory genes were downregulated in orbital fibroblasts, while LGMN, a promoter of ferroptosis, was upregulated. Thus, we hypothesize that TGF-β intervention could activate the TGF-β/SMAD2/3 signaling pathway, leading to ferroptosis in orbital fibroblasts, which is consistent with previous studies. We further employed C2 macrophage markers as seed genes in protein-protein interaction networks and performed restart random walk to identify hub genes driving C2 macrophage ferroptosis signaling. CD163 and LGMN were identified as consistent with previous findings. Additionally, using the DGIdb database, we investigated the interaction of top hub genes with drugs, revealing that HSP90AA1, HSP90AB1, and CSF1R interact with various drugs, suggesting they may serve as potential therapeutic targets for TAO.

Currently, research on ferroptosis and inflammation-immune related factors in Thyroid-Associated Ophthalmopathy (TAO) is limited, which presents certain limitations to our study. The single high-throughput chip and sequencing data used in this study were sourced from publicly available databases, where data uploaded by other researchers are relatively centralized. As a result, the clinical information available for each patient is quite limited, including factors such as age, sex, disease duration, previous treatment history, and clinical activity scores. This limits our ability to correlate gene expression with clinical characteristics, thus hindering a better association of gene expression with the clinical phenotype of the disease. Furthermore, our study on gene expression is still at the protein expression level, and the biological function of ferroptosis may be influenced by various molecular regulatory mechanisms. Moving forward, we aim to further investigate the regulatory mechanisms of TGF-β/SMAD2/3 axis activation in ferroptosis in orbital fibroblasts (OFs) in TAO and its association with the mechanism of orbital tissue fibrosis in TAO. Lastly, the potential therapeutic drugs identified are based solely on bioinformatic analysis, without in vivo or in vitro validation. Moreover, the toxicity of these drugs and whether they might cause damage to other tissues and organs will be a key focus of future research. In vivo and in vitro dual validation may be considered.

In conclusion, this study identified five differentially expressed ferroptosis-related genes (LGMN, CP1, FTL, MGST1, and NQO1) in the orbital connective tissues of TAO patients, contributing valuable insights to the study of ferroptosis in TAO. Cell-cell interaction analysis revealed the involvement of CD163 + macrophages and CCL-18 in TAO progression, highlighting them as potential molecular markers for disease prognosis. Finally, drug-target interaction analysis suggests that HSP90AA1, HSP90AB1, and CSF1R could be promising therapeutic targets for TAO.
